A 3D matchmove uses many image-feature tracks to infer the motion and orientation of the camera through a scene. Features with poor confidence or belonging to moving subjects should be filtered or masked before solving. The resulting camera path and point cloud require a useful scene origin and orientation, then a test object should be rendered to see whether it remains locked to the filmed environment. One- or two-point image transforms cannot supply the same depth-dependent motion. See [[Parallax as a 3D Matchmove Cue]].

A 3D sound emitter is the world-space source of a spatial sound. Its position and possibly its velocity determine how the sound reaches the [[3D Sound Listener]].

Distance can control attenuation, horizontal direction can influence stereo placement, and relative motion can produce a Doppler shift. Geometry between emitter and listener may also cause occlusion or obstruction.

A 3D sound listener represents the position and orientation from which the audio scene is heard. It is commonly associated with the camera or player, though the desired auditory viewpoint may differ from the visual one.

The audio engine compares the listener with each [[3D Sound Emitter]] to calculate direction, distance, relative velocity, and environmental effects for playback.

A 3D user interface is a [[User Interface]] that involves [[3D Interaction]]. It may combine spatial input, visual, auditory, or haptic output, and software mappings that let a person act in a real or [[Virtual Environment|virtual]] three-dimensional context.

Its main components are [[Input Device]]s, [[Output Device]]s, and [[Interaction Technique]]s. Common task families include [[3D Manipulation]], [[3D Travel]], [[Wayfinding]], and [[System Control]]. Good design requires these parts to work together; individually usable techniques do not automatically form a coherent interface.

3D interfaces appear in [[Virtual Reality]], [[Augmented Reality]], design, training, games, data analysis, medicine, collaboration, and [[Telerobotics]].
